Every forecast is worked out on this device by the physics behind VOACAP, a propagation model in use for decades. Nothing about your station or your path leaves the device.

Two models are offered, and the physics underneath is the same:

VOACAP, written by the US Institute for Telecommunication Sciences and reproduced faithfully here, defects included. It describes a typical day of the month, so 4 pm this Tuesday looks the same as 4 pm this Thursday.

Truecast, the default, works from what the ionosphere is doing on the day. Scored day by day against real measurements since 2015, it was closer than VOACAP on 77% of days.

Truecast runs VOACAP's physics against a daily sunspot figure worked out from ionosonde stations, a table of magnetic storms and a better estimate of the height a signal bounces from.

It was built and checked against ionosonde readings covering a whole solar cycle, then scored on eight months it had never seen. It removed the month-to-month bias VOACAP carries and was closer to the measured values in seven of them.

With no network it uses a built-in correction for the time of year, which still beats the monthly average. You can switch to VOACAP in Preferences at any time.

The sunspot number is the largest driver of the forecast: the bands, the hours and the paths all follow from it.

Figures for every month from {first} to {last} are built in, so a forecast needs no network. Months ahead use NOAA's published prediction.

When solar readings less than {hours} hours old are available, they are used instead.

A colour is the chance of making the contact, not how strong the signal will be. Reliable means about {reliable} times in 100 or better, patchy at least {patchy} in 100, and weak at least {weak} in 100. Below that the band counts as closed.\n\nThe numbers are corrected the way the HFcast project measured against months of real WSPR reports: VOACAP\'s daily swing and its day-to-day spread are both larger than what actually happens.

The map is centred on you: every straight line out from the middle is a great circle at its true bearing, and the distance from the middle is the true distance. The rim is the far side of the earth. Dashed rings are every 5,000 km.\n\nA rough map is drawn first, then a finer one of {points} places replaces it. Zoom in and more detail is worked out around what you are looking at.

Below a few hundred kilometres, the low bands work differently. The signal goes up steeply, comes back down near where it started, and there is no skip zone. Operators call this NVIS.\n\nHFPredict does not guess it from the distance. The engine works out the angle the signal leaves at, and a path counts as near-vertical when that angle is {degrees} degrees or more and the band works. The map marks that area with dots.
A note on the inverted V

VOACAP has no inverted V. HFPredict works one out as a dipole at {percent}% of the apex height, so a 10 m apex is modelled as a dipole 8 m up.\n\nThis is an approximation, not a measurement. A V with steep legs behaves lower than this, a shallow one higher. Choose the dipole if your wire is level.

The forecast is worked out on this device. Your station, antenna and path are never sent anywhere.\n\nWith the network on, three services see your IP address: NOAA for solar readings, GIRO for ionosonde measurements, and Open-Meteo when a place search finds too little in the built-in list (it also sees what you typed). Grid squares and coordinates are worked out on the device. Turn the network off in Preferences and nothing leaves at all.
